analysis.one_liner: Taxes coal, oil, and natural gas by their carbon content and returns the money through payroll tax rebates.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the House Ways and Means Committee without a hearing or a vote, one of hundreds of bills referred there in the 110th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would put a fee of $15 per ton of carbon dioxide on coal, petroleum products, and natural gas, rising about 10% a year plus inflation. The money would go into a trust fund: part for clean-energy research tax credits (up to $10 billion a year), part for transition aid to hard-hit industries (shrinking to zero by 2018), and the rest back to households as a credit against their payroll taxes, capped at what they paid in payroll tax or 10% of their Social Security benefits. Exports would be exempt, and companies that sequester carbon or run approved offset projects could claim refunds.
analysis.who_benefits: Working households would get the carbon fee money back through a credit against their payroll taxes, which for lower- and middle-income workers would likely exceed what they pay in higher energy prices. Social Security beneficiaries would get a credit worth 10% of their benefits. The clean-energy industry would gain up to $10 billion a year in research and investment tax credits.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Working households and Social Security recipients

how_it_helps.text: Most of the carbon fee revenue would be returned to individuals as a refundable credit against their payroll taxes, capped at the greater of their payroll taxes paid or 10% of Social Security benefits, so lower-earning workers get back more than the fee costs them.

The escalating fee starts at $15 per ton of carbon dioxide in 2008 and rises 10% a year plus inflation, giving producers and consumers a predictable, growing price signal to shift away from coal, oil, and natural gas.
Up to $10 billion a year (or one-sixth of the fund, whichever is smaller) would fund tax credits for clean-energy research, development, and investment.
Companies could claim refunds for carbon sequestered or for qualified offset projects that reduce or destroy greenhouse gases, excluding enhanced oil recovery.

analysis.who_pays: Coal, petroleum, and natural gas producers and importers would pay the fee, which they would pass along in higher prices for electricity, gasoline, and heating. Energy-intensive manufacturers would face higher input costs, softened by a temporary transition-assistance fund that phases out after 2017.
analysis.who_pays_short: Fossil fuel producers and energy consumers

drawbacks.text: Households would pay the carbon fee in higher energy prices immediately, while the rebate arrives only as an annual tax credit, creating a real cash-flow gap, and dependents claimed on someone else's return get no credit.

The rebate is capped at payroll taxes paid, so people with little or no payroll-tax liability other than the 10%-of-benefits rule for Social Security recipients would not be fully shielded from higher energy costs.

The fee rises every year indefinitely, and the transition aid for affected industries shrinks to zero by 2018, leaving coal-dependent regions and energy-intensive industries exposed to sustained cost increases.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The design is unusually progressive for a carbon tax: the money is recycled through payroll tax rebates, so most working households would come out ahead or even, while the burden falls hardest on fossil fuel producers and the heaviest energy users. The main honest cost is the timing gap between higher energy prices and the annual rebate, plus incomplete protection for households outside the payroll tax system.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced and sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John Larson introduced the bill on August 3, 2007.
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which holds jurisdiction over tax legislation.
No further action was taken on the bill for the rest of the 110th Congress, which ended January 3, 2009.
The bill had 12 cosponsors, all Democrats.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal, oil, and natural gas producers are better off because the escalating carbon fee never took effect, and energy consumers never faced the price increases it would have caused, though households also never received the payroll tax rebates.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil fuel producers avoided the carbon fee

for.name: Rep. John B. Larson
for.role: Sponsor, House Ways and Means Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the carbon tax and rebate bill on August 3, 2007.

against.name: House Committee on Ways and Means
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day of introduction and took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote; the only partisan signal is that the sponsor and all 12 cosponsors were Democrats, with no Republicans signed on.

industries.industry: Coal, oil, and natural gas producers
industries.note: The bill taxes each ton of carbon dioxide in coal, petroleum products, and natural gas at $15 starting in 2008, rising 10% a year plus inflation, with exports and sequestered carbon exempted. Their interest in stopping it ran against the bill's rebate to households.
The bill would fund up to $10 billion a year in tax credits for clean-energy research, development, and investment from the carbon fee revenue.

They would pay more for coal, petroleum, and natural gas as inputs, but a dedicated transition-assistance fund — 1/12 of the first year's revenue, phasing to zero by 2018 — would compensate negatively affected industries.
